When geographic monopolies are brought up, such as the location of harbors, mineral and natural resource deposits, natural barriers, they are often shrugged off. 'People will figure out other ways'. This seems to be losing track of the present by looking to the indefinite future, an ironic agreement with 'in the long run we're all dead'.

These asymmetries give rise to economic power disparities, which directly translate to political power on an international level. This is what geopolitics looks at - the emergence and exercise of power through resource availability and the ability to project force. It is not looking at relations through the lens of an ideology, seeking the most just policy. It is looking at relations through the lens of what is materially or culturally possible, and what actions can be taken as to make oneself more maneuverable and one's competitors less maneuverable. It is large scale organized competition.

Many visions of ancap seem to imply a post-geopolitical world. The vision is a world divided up into a patchwork of private property, with the organization to defend itself while not exercising regional policy towards some strategic objectives - and this isn't seen as a contradiction. Why is the organization towards some strategic objectives - defense - possible while others are not? Why does 'defense' follow the ancap specifications, why wouldn't it cover defense from economic threats too?

What are the geopolitics of ancap? How is the paradox resolved? Or, is the lack of a nation-esque body implementing regional strategic policy a requirement for ancap in the first place?

Capitalism is preferable to other economical systems because of how efficient resources are managed. So, what happens if one person owns the only gold mine or the only available harbour? Of course, he is in an economical advantage to other persons and needs to work less to make more profit. After all, he purchased (or inherited, which is basically the same) this harbour or mine and wants to make a profit out of it. Economical advantages due to clever investments should not be declared "unjust" at this point.

Problems arise, as soon as access to the harbour or a specific resource is denied or artificially expensive.
Artificially expensive services almost take care of themselves - if no one is willing or able to pay the price, the seller goes out of business or has to lower his prices. This may cripple innovation, but is a normal process for evaluating the worth of scarce material.
If the monopolist is not thinking economically or already has enough money, he can try to use his advantage to force "evil" contracts on people, who want to use the harbour to visit their family for christmas. In this case, he will be dealt with like he deals with others - he will be denied access to electricity and water, food from grocery stores, etc.

In contrast, a central unit or state can abuse and exploit these resources. Bribery will occur in the competition for resources, which are arbitrarily sold.
There is no real economic threat from private monopolies, who can not use force without facing consequences. Maybe every few years you will have to suffer for a few days from a mad businessman, who will return to business as usual because of the backlash happening. This may be uncomfortable, but poses no long term threat.
The organization of defense is different, because any human has a desire for safety. This does not only mean, that everyone will naturally try to cooperate, but a lack of defense at any time could be fatal. So, in this case there is always a consensus about what to do and also a need for instantaneuos reaction. Economic "threats" are clearly different from that.
